nodes.statement: Let \ textnormalU_n(cdot) \_n=0^infty be a sequence of random functions in C(D; E). The sequence \ textnormalU_n(cdot) \_n=0^infty is tight, if for any varepsilon > 0, there exists a compact set K subset C(D; E) such that mathbb P( textnormalU_n(cdot) in K ) ge 1 - varepsilon for any n.
nodes.raw_latex:
\label{defn:tight}
Let $\{ {\textnormal{U}}_{n}(\cdot) \}_{n=0}^\infty$ be a sequence of random functions in $C(D; E)$.
The sequence $\{ {\textnormal{U}}_{n}(\cdot) \}_{n=0}^\infty$ is \textit{tight}, if for any ${\varepsilon} > 0$, there exists a compact set $K \subset C(D; E)$ 
such that ${\mathbb P}( {\textnormal{U}}_{n}(\cdot) \in K ) \ge 1 - {\varepsilon}$ for any $n$.

nodes.label: defn:tight

\label{assump:smooth}
	There exists an operator $H\colon {\mathbb R}^{d_y}\rightarrow{\mathbb R}^{d_x}$ such that for any fixed $y\in{\mathbb R}^{d_y}$, $x = H(y)$ is the unique solution of
	
		$F(x,y) = 0$.    
		
	The operators $H$, $F$ and $G$ satisfy the following Lipschitz conditions: 
	$\forall\, x \in {\mathbb R}^{d_x}, y_{1}, y_{2} \in{\mathbb R}^{d_y}$,
	\begin{align}
		\|H(y_{1}) - H(y_{2})\| & \leq L_{H}\|y_{1}-y_{2}\|,\label{assump:smooth:FH:ineqH}\\
		\|F(x,y_1) - F(H(y_1),y_1)\| & \leq L_{F} \|x - H(y_1) \|, \nonumber    
		
		\\
		\|G(x,y_{1}) - G(H(y_{1}),y_{1})\| & \leq {L}_{G,x} \|x - H(y_{1})\|, \nonumber 
		
		\\   
		\| G(H(y_{1}),y_{1}) - G(H(y^\star), y^\star) \| & \leq {L}_{G,y} \| y - y^\star \|. \nonumber 
		
	\end{align}

\label{rema:fclt}
	For Theorem~\ref{thm:fclt-twotime}, we have the following explanations.
	\begin{enumerate}[(i)]
		\item \textbf{Ornstein-Uhlenbeck process}: 
		The drift terms in the SDEs \eqref{eq:fclt-twotime:x-sde} and \eqref{eq:fclt-twotime:y-sde} are linear, and the noise terms are constant. 
		As a result, the solution to these SDEs is a multi-dimensional Ornstein-Uhlenbeck process. Assumption~\ref{assump:hurwitz} ensures the uniqueness of the invariant distribution for these processes, with covariance matrices given in \eqref{eq:fclt-twotime:x-var} and \eqref{eq:fclt-twotime:y-var}~\citep[Section~6.5]{risken1996fokker}.
		
		\item \textbf{Stationary solution}:
		A ``stationary solution'' refers to a solution that is a stationary process. Specifically, this corresponds to a solution where the initial distribution matches the invariant distribution.
		
		\item \textbf{Interdependence}: The parameters $B_1$ and $\Sigma_{\xi}$ in \eqref{eq:fclt-twotime:x-sde} are associated solely with the fast-time-scale updates, indicating that the asymptotic behavior of the fast iterate resembles standard SA and is nearly unaffected by the slow iterate.
		In contrast, both $B_3$ and $\widetilde{\Sigma}_{\psi}$ in \eqref{eq:fclt-twotime:y-sde} are influenced by the slow-time-scale update.
		Specifically, $B_3$ (as detailed in Remark~\ref{remar:fclt:B-form}) involves the gradient of $F$, and $\widetilde{\Sigma}_{\psi}$ represents the asymptotic covariance of $\psi_{n} - B_2 B_1^{-1} \xi_{n}$.
		Decoupling ensures that the convergence rates of different iterates depend only on their respective step sizes. However, the fast-time-scale update still influences the slow-time-scale update through the constant terms, such as the coefficients in \eqref{eq:fclt-twotime:y-sde}.
		
		\item \textbf{Effect of step sizes}: The presence of $\tilde{\beta}$ in \eqref{eq:fclt-twotime:y-sde} highlights the impact of step sizes on asymptotic behavior. As illustrated in Example~\ref{exmp:fclt-stepsize}, for $\beta_{n} = \Theta(n^{-b})$ with $b \in (0,1]$, $\tilde{\beta} = \beta_{0}^{-1} \neq 0$ only when $b=1$, which requires the initial step size to be sufficiently large. This aligns with the convergence analysis for standard SA~\citep{moulines2011non}.
		Due to the assumption $\beta_{n} / \alpha_{n} = o(1)$, the choice of step sizes does not influence the asymptotic behavior in \eqref{eq:fclt-twotime:x-sde} (see Remark~\ref{rema:step-size}).
	\end{enumerate}

nodes.name: Comparison with previous work
nodes.statement: Compared to the FCLT presented in, which rescales the error terms hatx_n and haty_n using the square root of the fast-time-scale step size, we apply distinct rescalings to hatx_n and haty_n based on the square root of their respective step sizes. This refinement enables us to derive decoupled FCLTs under local linearity conditions, offering a more precise characterization of the asymptotic behavior in two-time-scale SA. Furthermore, our FCLTs can recover the classical CLTs from , as demonstrated in Corollary~.
nodes.raw_latex:
Compared to the FCLT presented in~\cite{faizal2023functional}, which rescales the error terms ${\hat{x}}_{n}$ and ${\hat{y}}_{n}$ using the square root of the fast-time-scale step size, we apply distinct rescalings to ${\hat{x}}_{n}$ and ${\hat{y}}_{n}$ based on the square root of their respective step sizes.
This refinement enables us to derive decoupled FCLTs under local linearity conditions, offering a more precise characterization of the asymptotic behavior in two-time-scale SA. Furthermore, our FCLTs can recover the classical CLTs from \cite{konda2004convergence, mokkadem2006convergence}, as demonstrated in Corollary~\ref{cor:clt}.

nodes.name: SGD with Polyak-Ruppert averaging
nodes.statement: Stochastic gradient descent (SGD), introduced by citeprobbins1951stochastic, iteratively updates the iterate x_t by~. To improve the convergence of SGD, an additional averaging step~ is often used~citeppolyak1992acceleration,ruppert1988efficient x_n+1 &= x_n - alpha_n(nabla f(x_n) + xi_n)~with~alpha_n = fracalpha_0 (n+1)^a ~(0 < a < 1) , \\ y_n+1 &= frac1n+1sum_tau=0^n x_tau = y_n - beta_n(y_n-x_n)~with~beta_n = frac1n+1. This update is a special case of with F(x, y) = nabla f(x), G(x, y) = y -x, H(y) equiv x^star and y^star = x_o^star. Contextualizing in Theorem~, one can check B_1 = nabla^2 f(x), B_3 - fractildebeta 2 I = frac12 I and widetildeSigma_psi = [ nabla^2 f(x_o^star) ]^-1 Sigma_xi [ nabla^2 f(x_o^star) ]^-1 . Thus, the solution to is Sigma_y = widetildeSigma_psi. We recover the CLT for the averaged iterate from and the FCLT for the original iterate from and . Additionally, our results offer a trajectory-level characterization for the averaged iterate.

nodes.name: SGD with momentum
nodes.statement: Stochastic heavy ball (SHB) is a variant of SGD based on momentum and adaptive step sizes and has been shown to be effective~citepgadat2018stochastic. A ``normalized'' version of SHB~citepgupal1972stochastic,gitman2019understanding iteratively runs x_n+1 &= x_n - alpha_n (x_n - nabla f(y_n) - xi_n),\\ y_n+1 &= y_n - beta_n x_n. This update is a special case of with F(x, y) = x-nabla f(y), G(x, y) = x, H(y) = nabla f(y), y^star = x_o^star and x^star = 0. Contextualizing this example in Theorem~, one can check B_1 = I, B_3 - fractildebeta2 I = nabla^2 f(x^star) - fractildebeta2 I and widetildeSigma_psi = Sigma_xi, implying that the asymptotic behavior is similar to that of standard SA. Consequently, for a strongly convex objective, the addition of momentum does not provide an asymptotic advantage over SGD. Furthermore, our result is not directly comparable to the FCLT in , as we consider distinct time scales, whereas their analysis focuses on a single-time-scale setting.

nodes.name: Gradient-based temporal-difference learning
nodes.statement: Gradient-based temporal-difference (TD) algorithms are widely used in off-policy reinforcement learning (RL), such as policy evaluation with function approximation~citepsutton2008convergent, sutton2009fast, maei2009convergent. We consider two specific algorithms: GTD2 and TDC with linear function approximation~citepsutton2009fast. These algorithms serve as typical examples of two-time-scale SA~citepdalal2018finite. For clarity, we concentrate on the specific update rules while omitting the details of the RL setup. A more comprehensive explanation is provided in Appendix~. In this problem, the goal is to estimate the value function V(s) for a given policy using a linear parameterization V(s; y) = phi(s)^top y, where phi(s) represents the feature vector of state s, and y denotes the parameter vector. Given i.i.d.\ samples \ (s_n, r_n, s'_n) \_n=0^infty~citepsutton2008convergent, where s_n is the current state, r_n is the reward and s'_n is the next state, the optimal parameter y can be estimated iteratively via the following update rulesfootnote Compared to the original formulation in , we incorporate an importance weight rho_n, the explicit form of which is provided in Appendix~. x_n+1 &= x_n - alpha_n big( phi(s_n)^top x_n - rho_n delta_n big) phi(s_n), \\ y_n+1 &= y_n - beta_n rho_n big( gamma phi(s'_n) - phi(s_n) big) phi(s_n)^top x_n, \ (GTD2) \\ y_n+1 &= y_n - beta_n rho_n big( gamma phi(s'_n) phi(s_n)^top x_n - delta_n phi(s_n) big), \ \, (TDC) where gamma is the discount factor, rho_n is the importance weight, and delta_n is the temporal-difference error defined as delta_n = r_n + ( gamma phi(s'_n) - phi(s_n) )^top y_n . Here, the fast iterate x_n is an auxiliary variable. Both GTD2 and TDC share the same fast time-scale update but differ in their slow time-scale updates. To contextualize these methods within the two-time-scale SA~, we define A_n = rho_n phi(s_n) ( phi(s_n) - gamma phi(s'_n) )^top , b_n = rho_n r_n phi(s_n) , C_n = phi(s_n) phi(s_n)^top , D_n = gamma rho_n phi(s_n) phi(s'_n)^top, and their expectations A= mathbb E[A_n], b = mathbb E[b_n], C=mathbb E[C_n], and D=mathbb E[D_n]. It can be checked that -- are an instance of with F(x,y) = Cx +Ay-b,\ \ G_GTD2(x,y) = -A^top x,\ \ G_TDC (x,y) = D^top x + Ay - b. It follows that H(y) = -C^-1(Ay-b), implying G_GTD2(H(y), y) = A^top C^-1 (Ay- b) and G_TDC(H(y), y) = (C - D^top) C^-1 (Ay - b). Although these expressions appear different, it can be verified that C - D^top = A^top citep[Equation~(68)]li2024high, leading to G_GTD2 (H(y), y) equiv G_TDC(H(y),y). Therefore, GTD2 and TDC have the same optimal solution, y^star = A^-1 b and x^star = H(y^star) = 0. Furthermore, the drift terms for both the methods in and are identical: B_1 = C and B_3 = A^top C^-1 A. For the noise terms, both the methods share the same noise for the fast time scale xi_n = C_n x_n + A_n y_n - b_n - F(x_n, y_n) . On the slow time scale, however, the noise differs slightly. For GTD2, the noise is expressed as psi^GTD2_n = - A_n^top x_n - G_GTD2(x_n, y_n) , whereas for TDC, it is given by psi^TDC_n = D_n^top x_n + A_n y_n - b_n - G_TDC(x_n, y_n). Despite these differences, both the methods ultimately result in the same diffusion term widetildeSigma_psi in . Additional details can be found in Appendix~. In summary, while GTD2 and TDC differ in form and may display distinct numerical behaviors~citepdann2014policy, they share identical asymptotic properties, aligning with the results of~citephu2024central. Compared to their work, our results provide a more detailed characterization of trajectory properties for i.i.d.\ samples.

\label{exmp:gtd}
	Gradient-based temporal-difference (TD) algorithms are widely used in off-policy reinforcement learning (RL), such as policy evaluation with function approximation~\citep{sutton2008convergent, sutton2009fast, maei2009convergent}.
	We consider two specific algorithms: GTD2 and TDC with linear function approximation~\citep{sutton2009fast}. These algorithms serve as typical examples of two-time-scale SA~\citep{dalal2018finite}. For clarity, we concentrate on the specific update rules while omitting the details of the RL setup. A more comprehensive explanation is provided in Appendix~\ref{append:exmp}.

	In this problem, the goal is to estimate the value function $V(s)$ for a given policy using a linear parameterization $V(s; y) = \phi(s)^\top y$, where $\phi(s)$ represents the feature vector of state $s$, and $y$ denotes the parameter vector.
	Given i.i.d.\ samples $\{ (s_n, r_n, s'_n) \}_{n=0}^\infty$~\citep{sutton2008convergent}, where $s_n$ is the current state, $r_n$ is the reward and $s'_n$ is the next state, the optimal parameter $y$ can be estimated iteratively via the following update rules\footnote{
	Compared to the original formulation in \cite{sutton2009fast}, we incorporate an importance weight $\rho_{n}$, the explicit form of which is provided in Appendix~\ref{append:exmp}.}
	\begin{align}
		x_{n+1} &= x_{n} - \alpha_{n} \big( \phi(s_{n})^{\top} x_{n} - \rho_{n} \delta_{n} \big) \phi(s_{n}), \label{eq:gtd-x}\\
		y_{n+1} &= y_{n} - \beta_{n} \rho_{n} \big( \gamma \phi(s'_{n}) - \phi(s_{n}) \big) \phi(s_{n})^\top x_{n}, \label{eq:gtd2-y}\  \qquad \mathrm{ (GTD2) }   \\
		y_{n+1} &= y_{n} - \beta_{n} \rho_{n} \big( \gamma \phi(s'_n) \phi(s_n)^\top x_{n} - \delta_{n} \phi(s_{n}) \big), \label{eq:tdc-y} \ \quad \,  \mathrm{ (TDC) }
	\end{align}
	where $\gamma$ is the discount factor, $\rho_{n}$ is the importance weight, and $\delta_{n}$ is the temporal-difference error defined as $	\delta_{n} = r_{n} + ( \gamma \phi(s'_{n}) - \phi(s_n) )^\top y_{n} $.
	Here, the fast iterate $x_{n}$ is an auxiliary variable.
	Both GTD2 and TDC share the same fast time-scale update but differ in their slow time-scale updates.
	
	To contextualize these methods within the two-time-scale SA~\eqref{alg:xy}, we define $A_n =  \rho_{n} \phi(s_n) ( \phi(s_n) - \gamma \phi(s'_n) )^\top $, $b_n = \rho_{n} r_{n} \phi(s_n) $, $C_n = \phi(s_{n}) \phi(s_n)^\top $, $D_n = \gamma \rho_{n} \phi(s_n) \phi(s'_n)^\top$, and their expectations $A= {\mathbb E}[A_n]$, $b = {\mathbb E}[b_n]$, $C={\mathbb E}[C_n]$, and $D={\mathbb E}[D_n]$.
	It can be checked that \eqref{eq:gtd-x} -- \eqref{eq:tdc-y} are an instance of \eqref{alg:xy} with
	\begin{equation*}
		F(x,y) = Cx +Ay-b,\ \ 
		G_{\mathrm{GTD2}}(x,y) = -A^\top x,\ \ 
		G_{\mathrm{TDC}} (x,y) = D^\top x + Ay - b.
	\end{equation*}


	It follows that $H(y) = -C^{-1}(Ay-b)$, implying
	$G_{\mathrm{GTD2}}(H(y), y) = A^\top C^{-1} (Ay- b)$ and $G_{\mathrm{TDC}}(H(y), y) = (C - D^\top) C^{-1} (Ay - b)$.
	Although these expressions appear different, it can be verified that $C - D^\top = A^\top$ \citep[Equation~(68)]{li2024high}, leading to $G_{\mathrm{GTD2}} (H(y), y) \equiv G_{\mathrm{TDC}}(H(y),y)$. 
	Therefore, GTD2 and TDC have the same optimal solution, $y^\star = A^{-1} b$ and $x^\star = H(y^\star) = 0$. Furthermore, the drift terms for both the methods in \eqref{eq:fclt-twotime:x-sde} and \eqref{eq:fclt-twotime:y-sde} are identical: $B_1 = C$ and $B_3 = A^\top C^{-1} A$.
	
	For the noise terms, both the methods share the same noise for the fast time scale $\xi_{n} = C_n x_{n} + A_n y_n - b_n - F(x_n, y_n) $.
	On the slow time scale, however, the noise differs slightly. For GTD2, the noise is expressed as $\psi^{\mathrm{GTD2}}_{n} = - A_{n}^\top x_n - G_{\mathrm{GTD2}}(x_n, y_n) $, whereas for TDC, it is given by $\psi^{\mathrm{TDC}}_{n} = D_n^\top x_{n} + A_n y_n - b_n - G_{\mathrm{TDC}}(x_n, y_n)$.
	Despite these differences, both the methods ultimately result in the same diffusion term $\widetilde{\Sigma}_{\psi}$ in \eqref{eq:fclt-twotime:y-sde}. Additional details can be found in Appendix~\ref{append:exmp}.
	
	In summary, while GTD2 and TDC differ in form and may display distinct numerical behaviors~\citep{dann2014policy}, they share identical asymptotic properties, aligning with the results of~\citep{hu2024central}. Compared to their work, our results provide a more detailed characterization of trajectory properties for i.i.d.\ samples.

It can be checked that -- are an instance of with F(x,y) = Cx +Ay-b,\ \ G_GTD2(x,y) = -A^top x,\ \ G_TDC (x,y) = D^top x + Ay - b. It follows that H(y) = -C^-1(Ay-b), implying G_GTD2(H(y), y) = A^top C^-1 (Ay- b) and G_TDC(H(y), y) = (C - D^top) C^-1 (Ay - b). Although these expressions appear different, it can be verified that C - D^top = A^top citep[Equation~(68)]li2024high, leading to G_GTD2 (H(y), y) equiv G_TDC(H(y),y). Therefore, GTD2 and TDC have the same optimal solution, y^star = A^-1 b and x^star = H(y^star) = 0. Furthermore, the drift terms for both the methods in and are identical: B_1 = C and B_3 = A^top C^-1 A. For the noise terms, both the methods share the same noise for the fast time scale xi_n = C_n x_n + A_n y_n - b_n - F(x_n, y_n) . On the slow time scale, however, the noise differs slightly. For GTD2, the noise is expressed as psi^GTD2_n = - A_n^top x_n - G_GTD2(x_n, y_n) , whereas for TDC, it is given by psi^TDC_n = D_n^top x_n + A_n y_n - b_n - G_TDC(x_n, y_n). Despite these differences, both the methods ultimately result in the same diffusion term widetildeSigma_psi in . Additional details can be found in Appendix~. In summary, while GTD2 and TDC differ in form and may display distinct numerical behaviors~citepdann2014policy, they share identical asymptotic properties, aligning with the results of~citephu2024central. Compared to their work, our results provide a more detailed characterization of trajectory properties for i.i.d.\ samples.

\label{rema:step-size}
We can derive the following results from Assumption~\ref{assump:stepsize-twotime}.
\begin{itemize}
    \item
    Assumption~\ref{assump:stepsize-twotime} implies $\beta_n = \Omega(1/n)$ and $\alpha_{n} / \beta_{n} = \omega(1)$. Then we have
        $\ssum{n}{0}{\infty} \alpha_{n} = \ssum{n}{0}{\infty} \beta_{n} = \infty$,
    which is a ubiquitous condition in the SA analysis to ensure convergence to the target solution \citep{konda2004convergence, doan2022nonlinear, faizal2023functional}.
    
    \item 
     Note that $\alpha_{n+1}^{-1} - \alpha_{n}^{-1} = \beta_{n+1}^{-1} \kappa_{n+1} - \beta_{n}^{-1} \kappa_{n} = \beta_{n+1}^{-1} (\kappa_{n+1} - \kappa_{n}) + \kappa_{n} ( \beta_{n+1}^{-1} - \beta_{n}^{-1} ) = \beta_{n+1}^{-1} \kappa_{n+1} ( 1 - \kappa_{n} / \kappa_{n+1} ) + \kappa_{n} ( \beta_{n+1}^{-1} - \beta_{n}^{-1} ) $.
    
    If we define  $\tilde{\alpha} := \lim_{n \to \infty} (\alpha_{n+1}^{-1} - \alpha_{n}^{-1} )$ then we have $\tilde{\alpha} = 0$. 
    This is why the choice of step sizes does not affect the SDE in \eqref{eq:fclt-twotime:x-sde}.
    The parameters $\tilde{\beta}$ and $\tilde{\alpha}$ also frequently in previous analysis \citep{konda2004convergence, faizal2023functional}.
    
    
\end{itemize}

nodes.name: Discussion on the interpolation
nodes.statement: For the way of interpolation in our works, also adopts the linear interpolation while uses two different interpolations for different parts. Since both alpha_N^alpha(n,t) and beta_N^beta(n,t) converge to 0 as n to infty, different interpolation methods make no difference in the asymptotic sense in our setup. We choose simple linear interpolation for analytical simplicity such that each trajectory is continuous in time.

For the way of interpolation in our works, \cite{faizal2023functional} also adopts the linear interpolation while \cite{gadat2018stochastic, liang2023asymptotic, blanchet2024limit} uses two different interpolations for different parts.

nodes.name: Proof of Lemma~\ref{lem:tight-twotime}
nodes.statement: We begin by proving the tightness of \ bartextnormalX_n(cdot) \_n=1^infty. The tightness of \ bartextnormalZ_n(cdot) \_n=1^infty can be established using a similar approach. Finally, we address the tightness of \ bartextnormalY_n(cdot) \_n=1^infty, which is the primary challenge in this proof. vspace0.2cm Part~1: tightness of \ bartextnormalX_n(cdot) \_n=1^infty. Note that Assumption~ implies mathbb E \| bartextnormalX_n(0) \|^2 = mathbb E \| checkx_n \|^2 = mathcal O(1). Then by Markov's inequality, the first condition in Proposition~ holds. Now we verify the second condition. Without loss of generality, assume 0 le t < s le T. From the definition of bartextnormalX_n(t) in , we have bartextnormalX_n(s) - bartextnormalX_n(t) & overset= checkx_N^alpha(n,s) + (s - underlines^alpha_n ) left( - B_1 checkx_N^alpha(n,s) + frac R_N^alpha(n,s)^x alpha_N^alpha(n,s) right) - fracs - underlines^alpha_n sqrt alpha_N^alpha(n,s) tildexi_N^alpha(n,s) \\ & - checkx_N^alpha(n,t) - (t - underlinet^alpha_n ) left( - B_1 checkx_N^alpha(n,t) + frac R_N^alpha(n,t)^x alpha_N^alpha(n,t) right) + fract - underlinet^alpha_n sqrtalpha_N^alpha(n,t) tildexi_N^alpha(n,t) \\ & overset= Bigg\ ssumkN^alpha(n,t)N^alpha(n,s)-1 alpha_k left( - B_1 checkx_k + fracR_k^xalpha_k right) - (t - underlinet^alpha_n ) left( - B_1 checkx_N^alpha(n,t) + frac R_N^alpha(n,t)^x alpha_N^alpha(n,t) right) \\ & + (s - underlines^alpha_n ) left( - B_1 checkx_N^alpha(n,s) + frac R_N^alpha(n,s)^x alpha_N^alpha(n,s) right) Bigg\ - Bigg\ ssumkN^alpha(n,t)N^alpha(n,s)-1 sqrtalpha_k tildexi_k \\ & - fract - underlinet^alpha_n sqrtalpha_N^alpha(n,t) tildexi_N^alpha(n,t) + fracs - underlines^alpha_n sqrt alpha_N^alpha(n,s) tildexi_N^alpha(n,s) Bigg\ \\ & =: B^(1x,n)_t,s - mboxboldmathXiunboldmath^(n)_t,s. For the first term, noting that t' - (underlinet')^alpha_n le alpha_N^alpha(n,t') for t'=t,s, we have \| B^(1x,n)_t,s \| & le ssumkN^alpha(n,t)N^alpha(n,s) - 1 alpha_k left\| B_1 checkx_k - fracR_k^xalpha_k right\| + (s - underlines^alpha_n) left\| B_1 checkx_N^alpha(n,s) - frac R_N^alpha(n,s)^x alpha_N^alpha(n,s) right\| nonumber \\ & le ssumkN^alpha(n,t)N^alpha(n,s) alpha_k left\| B_1 checkx_k - fracR_k^xalpha_k right\|. By Assumption~ and Lemma~, we have that sup_n mathbb E left\| B_1 checkx_n - fracR_n^x alpha_n right\|^2 le 2 \| B_1 \|^2 sup_n mathbb E \| checkx_n \|^2 + 2 sup_n frac mathbb E \| R_n^x \|^2alpha_n^2 le C^ti_x for some C^ti_x > 0. Applying the Cauchy-Schwarz inequality, we obtain mathbb E \| B^(1x,n)_t,s \|^2 & oversetle mathbb E left( ssumkN^alpha(n,t)N^alpha(n,s) alpha_k left\| B_1 checkx_k - fracR_k^xalpha_k right\|right)^2 nonumber \\ & le left( ssumkN^alpha(n,t)N^alpha(n,s) alpha_k right) left( ssumkN^alpha(n,t)N^alpha(n,s) alpha_k mathbb E left\| B_1 checkx_k - fracR_k^xalpha_k right\|^2 right) nonumber \\ & overset le C^ti_x left( ssumkN^alpha(n,t)N^alpha(n,s) alpha_k right)^2 le C^ti_x ( s-t + 2 alpha_n )^2 overset(a)le K_1(s-t)^2, where there exists K_1 such that (a) holds for any n because alpha_n to 0. For the second term, with p in left(2, frac41 + ( delta_H vee delta_F vee delta_G )/2 right], we have mathbb E \| mboxboldmathXiunboldmath^(n)_t,s \|^p & oversetle C^ti_p left[ N^alpha(n, s) - N^alpha(n,t) + 1 right]^fracp2-1 ssumk N^alpha(n,t) N^alpha(n,s) alpha_k^fracp2 mathbb E \| tildexi_k \|^p, where we have used t' - underlinet'^alpha_n le alpha_N^alpha(n,t') for t'=t,s and Burkholder's inequality in the following proposition with C^ti_p = left[ (p-1) vee frac1p-1 right]^p. [Burkholder's inequality, ] Fix any p ge 2. Let \ X_k \_1 le k le n be a finite mathbb R^d-valued martingale difference sequence with sup_1 le k le n mathbb E \| X_k \|^p < infty. Then we have mathbb E left\| ssumk1n X_k right\|^p le left[ (p-1) vee frac1p-1 right]^p mathbb E left( ssumk1n \| X_k \|^2 right)^fracp2, which together with Jensen's inequality imply mathbb E left\| ssumk1n X_k right\|^p le left[ (p-1) vee frac1p-1 right]^p n^fracp2 - 1 mathbb E ssumk1n \| X_k \|^p. From the definition of tildexi_k and Assumption~, there exists C^ti_xi > 0 such that sup_k mathbb E \| tildexi_k \|^p le C^ti_xi . It follows that mathbb E \| mboxboldmathXiunboldmath^(n)_t,s \|^p & le C^ti_p C^ti_xi left( frac s-t + 2alpha_n alpha_ N^alpha(n, s) + 1 right)^fracp2-1 alpha_n^ fracp2 - 1 ssumk N^alpha(n,t) N^alpha(n,s) alpha_k nonumber \\ & le C^ti_p C^ti_xi ( s-t + 3 alpha_n )^fracp2 left( frac alpha_n alpha_ N^alpha(n, s) right)^fracp2-1 nonumber \\ & overset (a) le C^ti_p C^ti_xi C^ti_alpha ( s-t + 3 alpha_n )^fracp2 overset (b) le K_2 ( s-t )^fracp2, where (a) uses Lemma~ with C^ti_alpha = 2^ ( lceil 2T/ c_alpha rceil + 1 )(p/2-1) with c_alpha specified therein, and there exists K_2 such that (b) holds for any n. Combining and with Markov's inequality, we have mathbb P left( \| bartextnormalX_n(s) - bartextnormalX_n(t) \| ge varepsilon right) & le mathbb P left( \| B^(1x,n)_t,s \| ge fracvarepsilon2 right) + mathbb P left( \| mboxboldmathXiunboldmath^(n)_t,s \| ge fracvarepsilon2 right) \\ & le frac4varepsilon^2 mathbb E \| B^(1x,n)_t,s \| ^2 + frac2^pvarepsilon^p mathbb E \| mboxboldmathXiunboldmath^(n)_t,s \|^p \\ & le 8 (K_1 vee K_2) left[ frac (s-t)^2 varepsilon^2 + frac (s-t)^fracp2 varepsilon^p right]. This upper bound verifies the second condition in Proposition~. Consequently, \ bartextnormalX_n(cdot) \_n=1^infty is tight. vspace0.2cm Part~2: the tightness of \ bartextnormalZ_n(cdot) \_n=1^infty. Note that in the proof of Part~1, the only place we employed Lemma~ is and in fact, we only require mathbb E \| R_n^x \|^2 = mathcal O(alpha_n^2). Moreover, the dimension d_x would not affect the proof. The tightness of \ bartextnormalZ_n(cdot) \_n=1^infty follows from a similar procedure by applying the residual bounds in Lemma~. vspace0.2cm Part~3: the tightness of \ bartextnormalY_n(cdot) \_n=1^infty. Note that Assumption~ implies mathbb E \| bartextnormalY_n(0) \|^2 = mathbb E \| checky_n \|^2 = mathcal O(1). Then by Markov's inequality, the first condition in Proposition~ holds. Now we verify the second condition. Without loss of generality, we assume 0 le t < s le T. For ease of notation, we define widetildeB_3 := B_3 - fractildebeta I2. From the definition of bartextnormalY_n(t) in , we have bartextnormalY_n(s) - bartextnormalY_n(t) & overset= checky_N^beta(n,s) + (s - underlines^beta_n ) left( - widetildeB_3 checky_N^beta(n,s) + frac R_N^beta(n,s)^y beta_N^beta(n,s) right) - fracs - underlines^beta_n sqrt beta_N^beta(n,s) psi_N^beta(n,s) \\ & - checky_N^beta(n,t) - (t - underlinet^beta_n ) left( - widetildeB_3 checky_N^beta(n,t) + frac R_N^beta(n,t)^y beta_N^beta(n,t) right) + fract - underlinet^beta_n sqrt beta_N^beta(n,t) psi_N^beta(n,t) \\ & - (s - underlines^beta_n) sqrt frac alpha_N^beta(n,s) beta_N^beta(n,s) B_2 checkx_N^beta(n,s) + (t - underlinet^beta_n) sqrt frac alpha_N^beta(n,t) beta_N^beta(n,t) B_2 checkx_N^beta(n,t) \\ & overset= Bigg\ ssumkN^beta(n,t)N^beta(n,s)-1 beta_k left( - widetildeB_3 checky_k + fracR_k^ybeta_k right) - (t - underlinet^beta_n ) left( - widetildeB_3 checky_N^beta(n,t) + frac R_N^beta(n,t)^y beta_N^beta(n,t) right) \\ & + (s - underlines^beta_n ) left( - widetildeB_3 checky_N^beta(n,s) + frac R_N^beta(n,s)^y beta_N^beta(n,s) right) Bigg\ - Bigg\ ssumkN^beta(n,t)N^beta(n,s)-1 sqrtbeta_k psi_k \\ & - fract - underlinet^beta_n sqrtbeta_N^beta(n,t) psi_N^beta(n,t) + fracs - underlines^beta_n sqrtbeta_N^beta(n,s) psi_N^beta(n,s) Bigg\ - Bigg\ ssumkN^beta(n,t)N^beta(n,s)-1 beta_k sqrt fracalpha_kbeta_k B_2 checkx_k \\ & - (t - underlinet^beta_n) sqrt frac alpha_N^beta(n,t) beta_N^beta(n,t) B_2 checkx_N^beta(n,t) + (s - underlines^beta_n) sqrt frac alpha_N^beta(n,s) beta_N^beta(n,s) B_2 checkx_N^beta(n,s) Bigg\ \\ & =: B^(3y,n)_t,s - mboxboldmathPsiunboldmath^(n)_t,s - B^(2x,n)_t,s. For the first and second terms, similar to the derivation of and , with p in left(2, frac41 + ( delta_H vee delta_F vee delta_G )/2 right], there exist K_3, K_4 such that for any n, mathbb E \| B^(3y,n)_t,s \|^2 le K_3 (s-t)^2 and mathbb E \| mboxboldmathPsiunboldmath^(n)_t,s \|^p le K_4 (s-t)^fracp2. Main difficulty. The main difficulty lies to how to deal with the last term B^(2x,n)_t,s. nodes.name: Proof of Lemma~\ref{lem:slow:stepsize-aux}
nodes.statement: For ease of notation, we define n_0 := N^beta(n, t) and n_1 := N^beta(n, s)-1. Since the real parts of the eigenvalues of B_1 are no less than mu_1, beta_j = o(alpha_j) and n is sufficiently large, we have \| A_j \| le \| I - alpha_j B_1 \| + beta_j \| H^star B_2 \| le 1 - mu_1 alpha_j / 2 for any j > l ge n. It follows that left\| sum_k=l+1^n_1 sqrtbeta_k prod_i=1^k-l-1 A_k-i right\| le sum_k=l+1^n_1 sqrtbeta_k prod_i=l+1^k-1 left( 1 - frac mu_1 alpha_i 2 right) le sum_k=l+1^n_1 sqrtbeta_k exp left( - fracmu_12 sum_i=l+1^k-1 alpha_i right). nodes.name: Proof of Lemma~\ref{lem:mart-prob-twotime}
nodes.statement: We first prove Part~(i). For convenience, with Gamma^alpha_n,m introduced in Definition~, we define the following notation barN^alpha(n, t) := min left\ m ge n colon Gamma^alpha_n, m ge t right\. Then the filtration defined in can be written succinctly as mathcal F^bartextnormalX_n,t = mathcal F_ barN^alpha(n, t) . We construct mathcal M_n^f(t) as mathcal M_n^f(t) = ssumknbarN^alpha(n,t)-1 big\ f(checkx_k+1) - f(checkx_k) - mathbb E[ f(checkx_k+1) - f(checkx_k) | mathcal F_k ] big\. Clearly, mathcal M_n^f(t) is adapted to the filtration (mathcal F^bartextnormalX_n,t)_t ge 0. Next we verify that mathcal M_n^f(t) is a martingale w.r.t. (mathcal F^bartextnormalX_n,t)_t ge 0. For any t > s ge 0, if k le barN^alpha(n,s)-1, then checkx_k, checkx_k+1 in mathcal F^bartextnormalX_n,s and mathcal F_k subset mathcal F^bartextnormalX_n,s, implying \[ mathbb E big\ f(checkx_k+1) - f(checkx_k) - mathbb E[ f(checkx_k+1) - f(checkx_k) | mathcal F_k ] big| mathcal F^bartextnormalX_n,s big\ = f(checkx_k+1) - f(checkx_k) - mathbb E[ f(checkx_k+1) - f(checkx_k) | mathcal F_k ]. \] Otherwise, k ge barN^alpha(n,s) and mathcal F^bartextnormalX_n,s subseteq mathcal F_k, implying \[ mathbb E big\ f(checkx_k+1) - f(checkx_k) - mathbb E[ f(checkx_k+1) - f(checkx_k) | mathcal F_k ]\, big|\, mathcal F^bartextnormalX_n,s big\ = 0. \] Consequently, mathbb E [ mathcal M_n^f(t) | mathcal F^bartextnormalX_n,s ] & = ssumknbarN^alpha(n,t)-1 mathbb E big\ f(checkx_k+1) - f(checkx_k) - mathbb E[ f(checkx_k+1) - f(checkx_k) | mathcal F_k ]\, big|\, mathcal F^bartextnormalX_n,s big\ \\ & = ssumknbarN^alpha(n,s)-1 big\ f(checkx_k+1) - f(checkx_k) - mathbb E[ f(checkx_k+1) - f(checkx_k) | mathcal F_k ] big\ = mathcal M_n^f(s), which implies that mathcal M_n^f (t) is a martingale w.r.t.\ mathcal F^bartextnormalX_n,t. Now we focus on the residual term mathcal R_n^f(t). For notational simplicity, we define overlinet^alpha_n = Gamma^alpha_n, barN^alpha(n,t) . Then we have overlinet^alpha_n - alpha_barN^alpha(n,t) - 1 < t le overlinet^alpha_n. With this notation and underlinet^alpha_n introduced in Definition~,footnoteIn the notation underlinet^alpha_n, we view t as a variable. mathcal R_n^f(t) can be expressed as mathcal R_n^f(t) & = f( bartextnormalX_n(t) ) - f(bartextnormalX_n(0) ) - int_0^t mathcal A^x f( bartextnormalX_n(s) )\, d s - mathcal M_n ^f(t) nonumber \\ & overset= f(bartextnormalX_n(t)) - f(bartextnormalX_n(overlinet^alpha_n) ) - int_0^t mathcal A^x f(bartextnormalX_n(s)) \,d s + ssumknbarN^alpha(n,t)-1 mathbb E [ f(checkx_k+1) - f(checkx_k) | mathcal F_k ] nonumber \\ & overset= f(bartextnormalX_n(t)) - f(bartextnormalX_n(overlinet^alpha_n) ) - int_0^t mathcal A^x f(bartextnormalX_n(s)) \,d s + ssumknbarN^alpha(n,t)-1 left( alpha_k mathcal A^x f(checkx_k) + R^f_k right) nonumber \\ & overset(a)= f(bartextnormalX_n(t)) - f(bartextnormalX_n(overlinet^alpha_n) ) + int_0^overlinet^alpha_n left( mathcal A^x f(bartextnormalX_n(underlines^alpha_n) ) - mathcal A^x f(bartextnormalX_n(s)) right) \,d s nonumber \\ & + int_t^overlinet^alpha_n mathcal A^x f(bartextnormalX_n(s)) \,d s + ssumknbarN^alpha(n,t) - 1 R^f_k, where for step (a), we used Fact~~ such that alpha_k mathcal A^x f(checkx_k) = int_Gamma^alpha_n,k^Gamma^alpha_n,k+1 mathcal A^x f( bartextnormalX_n( underlines^alpha_n ) ) \,d s . Notice that f in C_c^2(mathbb R^d_x). For a fixed t, to control mathcal R_n^f(t) in the L_1 sense, we need to control the following L_1 distances mathbb E \| bartextnormalX_n(s) - bartextnormalX_n( underlines^alpha_n ) \| and mathbb E \| bartextnormalX_n(s) - bartextnormalX_n( overlines^alpha_n ) \| for any s in [0,overlinet_n^alpha]. From the definition of bartextnormalX_n(cdot) in , we have bartextnormalX_n( underlines^alpha_n ) = checkx_N^alpha(n,s). Consequently, bartextnormalX_n(s) - bartextnormalX_n( underlines^alpha_n ) = (s - underlines^alpha_n ) left(- B_1 checkx_N^alpha(n,s) + fracR^x_N^alpha (n,s) alpha_N^alpha (n,s) right) - fracs - underlines^alpha_n sqrt alpha_N^alpha(n,s) tildexi_N^alpha(n,s). It follows that for each s in [0, overlinet_n^alpha] , the following results hold mathbb E \| bartextnormalX_n(s) - bartextnormalX_n( underlines^alpha_n ) \| & le (s - underlinet^alpha_n ) mathbb E left\| - B_1 checkx_N^alpha(n,s) + fracR^x_N^alpha (n,s) alpha_N^alpha (n,s) right\| + fracs - underlines^alpha_n sqrt alpha_N^alpha(n,s) mathbb E \| tildexi_N^alpha(n,s) \| \\ & oversetlesssim (s - underlines^alpha_n ) + sqrts - underlines^alpha_n lesssim sqrt alpha_N^alpha(n,s) , \\ mathbb E \| bartextnormalX_n(s) - bartextnormalX_n( overlines^alpha_n ) \| & le mathbb E \| bartextnormalX_n(s) - bartextnormalX_n( underlines^alpha_n ) \| + mathbb E \| bartextnormalX_n( overlines^alpha_n ) - bartextnormalX_n( underlines^alpha_n ) \| \\ & le mathbb E \| bartextnormalX_n(s) - bartextnormalX_n( underlines^alpha_n ) \| + ( overlines^alpha_n - underlines^alpha_n ) mathbb E left\| - B_1 checkx_N^alpha(n,s) + fracR^x_N^alpha (n,s) alpha_N^alpha (n,s) right\| \\ & + frac overlines^alpha_n - underlines^alpha_n sqrt alpha_N^alpha(n,s) mathbb E \| tildexi_N^alpha(n,s) \| \\ & lesssim sqrt alpha_N^alpha(n,s) . Since f in C_c^2(mathbb R^d_x), it follows that mathbb E | f(bartextnormalX_n(t)) - f(bartextnormalX^(n)_overlinet^alpha_n) | & lesssim mathbb E \| bartextnormalX_n(t) - bartextnormalX^(n)_overlinet^alpha_n \| lesssim sqrtalpha_N^alpha(n,t) = o(1), \\ mathbb E left| int_t^overlinet^alpha_n mathcal A^x f(bartextnormalX_n(s)) \,d s right| & lesssim int_t^overlinet^alpha_n 1 \,d s = o(1), \\ mathbb E left| int_0^overlinet^alpha_n left( mathcal A^x f(bartextnormalX_n (underlines^alpha_n) ) - mathcal A^x f(bartextnormalX_n(s)) right) \,d s right| & lesssim int_0^overlinet^alpha_n mathbb E \| bartextnormalX_n(s) - bartextnormalX_n (underlines^alpha_n ) \| \,d s \\ & lesssim int_0^overlinet^alpha_n sqrtalpha_N^alpha(n,s) ds lesssim sqrtalpha_n = o(1). Moreover, for a fixed t, Lemma~ implies mathbb E left| ssumknbarN^alpha(n,t) - 1 R^f_k right| le ssumknbarN^alpha(n,t) - 1 alpha_k mathbb E left| fracR^f_kalpha_k right| le sup_k' ge n mathbb E left| fracR^f_k'alpha_k' right| cdot ssumknbarN^alpha(n,t) - 1 alpha_k lesssim o(1). Plugging and into yields that for a fixe t, mathbb E | mathcal R_n^f(t) | to 0 as n to infty. vspace0.2cm For Part~(ii), we similarly define barN^beta(n, t) := min left\ m ge n colon Gamma^beta_n, m ge t right\ and mathcal M_n^g(t) = ssumknbarN^beta(n,t)-1 big\ f(checkz_k+1) - f(checkz_k) - mathbb E[ f(checkz_k+1) - f(checkz_k) | mathcal F_k ] big\. The remaining proof is similar to that of Part~(i).

nodes.statement: The proof is divided into three steps. In the first step, we apply Proposition~ to establish the convergence of convergent subsequences. In the second step, we verify Condition~ in Proposition~. Finally, we apply Proposition~ to establish the convergence of the whole sequence. vspace0.2cm Step~1: establishing subsequence convergence. For the conditions in Proposition~, Condition~ has been discussed in Section~. Lemma~ ensures that Condition~ holds. To verify Condition~, we apply Lemma~, which shows that for any f in C^2_c(mathbb R^d_x) and t ge 0, one has that f(bartextnormalX_n(t)) - f(bartextnormalX_n(0)) - int_0^t mathcal A^x f(bartextnormalX_n(s)) ds = mathcal M_n^f(t) + mathcal R_n^f(t), where for each n, mathcal M_n^f(t) is a martingale w.r.t.\ (mathcal F^bartextnormalX_n,t)_t ge 0 defined in and for each t, mathbb E | mathcal R_n^f(t) | to 0 as n to infty. Then for any k ge 0, 0 le t_1 < t_2 < dots < t_k le t le t+s , and f, h_1, h_2, dots, h_k in C_c^2(mathbb R^d_x) & \ Bigg|\, mathbb E bigg[ Big( f(bartextnormalX_n(t+s)) - f(bartextnormalX_n(t)) - int_t^t+s mathcal A^x f(bartextnormalX_n(r)) dr Big) prod_i=1^k h_i(bartextnormalX_n(t_i)) bigg]\, Bigg| \\ & = Bigg|\, mathbb E bigg[ big(mathcal M_n^f(t+s) - mathcal M_n^f(t) + mathcal R_n^f(t+s) - mathcal R_n^f(t) big) prod_i=1^k h_i(bartextnormalX_n(t_i)) bigg] \, Bigg| \\ & = Bigg|\, mathbb E bigg\ prod_i=1^k h_i(bartextnormalX_n(t_i))\, mathbb E big[ mathcal M_n^f(t+s) - mathcal M_n^f(t) + mathcal R_n^f(t+s) - mathcal R_n^f(t) \,big|\, mathcal F_n,t^bartextnormalX big] bigg\ \, Bigg| \\ & le mathbb E bigg\ prod_i=1^k | h_i(bartextnormalX_n(t_i)) | \, mathbb E big[ | mathcal R_n^f(t+s) | + | mathcal R_n^f(t) | \,big|\, mathcal F_n,t^bartextnormalX big] bigg\ to 0 as n to infty. Now we assume \ bartextnormalX_n_k (cdot) \_k=1^infty is a weakly convergent subsequence of \ bartextnormalX_n (cdot) \_n=1^infty. Clearly, this subsequence satisfies Condition~ in Proposition~. Suppose bartextnormalX_n_k (0) Rightarrow tildepi. Then Proposition~ ensures that bartextnormalX_n_k(cdot) Rightarrow textnormalX^tildepi(cdot) as k to infty, where textnormalX^tildepi(cdot) is the solution of the SDE in with the initial distribution tildepi. vspace0.2cm Step~2: verifying initial conditions. To establish the convergence of bartextnormalX_n(0), it suffices to prove that all the convergent subsequences have the same limit. In fact, this limit is pi^star, the unique invariant distribution of . The uniqueness is guaranteed by Proposition~. In the next, we prove that if the subsequence bartextnormalX_n_k(0) Rightarrow tildepi, one must have tildepi = pi^star. The proof is divided to the following two parts: (i) for any fixed T > 0, we show that there exists a solution textnormalX(t) to such that tildepi has the same distribution as textnormalX(T); (ii) when T is sufficiently large, the geometric ergodicity implies that the distribution of textnormalX(T) can be arbitrarily close to pi^star. Part (i). We first introduce some additional notation. Recall that Gamma^alpha_n,n' = ssumknn'-1 alpha_k. For n in mathbb N and t ge 0, we define M^alpha (n,t) := minleft\ m ge 0 colon Gamma^alpha_m,n le t right\\ and \ tildet^alpha_n := Gamma^alpha_M^alpha(n,t), n. Since alpha_n to 0, we have tildet^alpha_n uparrow t. For a fixed T>0, we consider the subsequence \ bartextnormalX_M^alpha(n_k, T)(cdot) \_k=0^infty, which satisfies bartextnormalX_M^alpha(n_k, T)(0) = checkx_M^alpha(n_k, T) \ and \ bartextnormalX_M^alpha(n_k, T)( widetildeT^alpha_n_k)= checkx_n_k, where widetildeT^alpha_n := Gamma^alpha_M^alpha(n,T), n By Lemma~, \ bartextnormalX_n(t) \_n=1^infty is tight. Then Prokhorov's theorem (i.e., Proposition~~) implies that the subsequence \ bartextnormalX_M^alpha(n_k, T)(cdot) \_k=0^infty further has a weakly convergent subsequence. Without loss of generality, we assume the subsequence \ bartextnormalX_M^alpha(n_k, T)(cdot) \_k=0^infty itself weakly converges. Then its initial distribution sequence also converges weakly, i.e., checkx_M^alpha(n_k, T) Rightarrow mu_T for some distribution mu_T. Consequently, we also have bartextnormalX_M^alpha(n_k, T)(T) Rightarrow textnormalX^mu_T(T). Moreover, recall that we have verified the second condition of Proposition~ in the proof of Lemma~. Then |T - widetildeT^alpha_n_k| to 0 implies that left\| bartextnormalX_M^alpha(n_k, T)(widetildeT^alpha_n_k) - bartextnormalX_M^alpha(n_k, T)(T) right\| oversetprightarrow 0 as k to infty.     Then for any $k \ge 0$, $0 \le t_1 < t_2 < \dots < t_k \le t \le t+s $, and $f, h_1, h_2, \dots, h_k \in C_c^2({\mathbb R}^{d_x})$
    \begin{align*}
        & \quad \ \Bigg|\, {\mathbb E}  \bigg[ \Big( f({\bar{\textnormal{X}}}_{n}(t+s)) - f({\bar{\textnormal{X}}}_{n}(t)) - \int_t^{t+s} {\mathcal A}^x f({\bar{\textnormal{X}}}_{n}(r)) dr \Big) \prod_{i=1}^k h_i({\bar{\textnormal{X}}}_{n}(t_i)) \bigg]\, \Bigg| \\
        & = \Bigg|\, {\mathbb E} \bigg[ \big({\mathcal M}_{n}^f(t+s) - {\mathcal M}_{n}^f(t) + {\mathcal R}_{n}^f(t+s) - {\mathcal R}_{n}^f(t) \big) \prod_{i=1}^k h_i({\bar{\textnormal{X}}}_{n}(t_i)) \bigg] \, \Bigg| \\
        & = \Bigg|\, {\mathbb E} \bigg\{ \prod_{i=1}^k h_i({\bar{\textnormal{X}}}_{n}(t_i))\, {\mathbb E} \big[ {\mathcal M}_{n}^f(t+s) - {\mathcal M}_{n}^f(t) + {\mathcal R}_{n}^f(t+s) - {\mathcal R}_{n}^f(t) \,\big|\, {\mathcal F}_{n,t}^{\bar{\textnormal{X}}} \big]  \bigg\} \, \Bigg| \\
        & \le  {\mathbb E} \bigg\{ \prod_{i=1}^k | h_i({\bar{\textnormal{X}}}_{n}(t_i)) | \, {\mathbb E} \big[ | {\mathcal R}_{n}^f(t+s) | + | {\mathcal R}_{n}^f(t) | \,\big|\, {\mathcal F}_{n,t}^{\bar{\textnormal{X}}} \big]  \bigg\} \to 0
    \end{align*}
    as $n \to \infty$.
    Now we assume $ \{ {\bar{\textnormal{X}}}_{n_k} (\cdot) \}_{k=1}^\infty $ is a weakly convergent subsequence of $ \{ {\bar{\textnormal{X}}}_{n} (\cdot) \}_{n=1}^\infty$.
    Clearly, this subsequence satisfies Condition~\ref{prop:final:condition:initial} in Proposition~\ref{prop:mart-prob-approx}.
    Suppose ${\bar{\textnormal{X}}}_{n_k} (0) \Rightarrow \tilde{\pi}$. Then Proposition~\ref{prop:mart-prob-approx} ensures that ${\bar{\textnormal{X}}}_{n_k}(\cdot) \Rightarrow {\textnormal{X}}^{\tilde{\pi}}(\cdot)$ as $k \to \infty$, where ${\textnormal{X}}^{\tilde{\pi}}(\cdot)$ is the solution of the SDE in \eqref{eq:fclt-twotime:y-sde} with the initial distribution $\tilde\pi$.
    \vspace{0.2cm}
    
    \textbf{Step~2: verifying initial conditions}. 
    To establish the convergence of ${\bar{\textnormal{X}}}_{n}(0)$, it suffices to prove that all the convergent subsequences have the same limit.
    In fact, this limit is $\pi^\star$, the unique invariant distribution of \eqref{eq:fclt-twotime:y-sde}. The uniqueness is guaranteed by Proposition~\ref{prop:ergo}.
    In the next, we prove that if the subsequence ${\bar{\textnormal{X}}}_{n_k}(0) \Rightarrow \tilde{\pi}$, one must have $\tilde{\pi} = \pi^\star$. 
    The proof is divided to the following two parts: (i) for any fixed $T > 0$, we show that there exists a solution ${\textnormal{X}}(t)$ to \eqref{eq:fclt-twotime:x-sde} such that $\tilde{\pi}$ has the same distribution as ${\textnormal{X}}(T)$;
    (ii) when $T$ is sufficiently large, the geometric ergodicity implies that the distribution of ${\textnormal{X}}(T)$ can be arbitrarily close to $\pi^\star$.
    
    
    \textbf{Part (i)}.
    We first introduce some additional notation.
    Recall that $\Gamma^\alpha_{n,n'} = \ssum{k}{n}{n'-1} \alpha_k$.
    For $n \in {\mathbb N}$ and $t \ge 0$, we define 
    \begin{align*}
        M^\alpha (n,t) := \min\left\{ m \ge 0 \colon \Gamma^\alpha_{m,n} \le t \right\}\ \text{ and } \
        \tilde{t}^\alpha_{n} := \Gamma^\alpha_{M^\alpha(n,t), n}.
    \end{align*}
    
    
    Since $\alpha_{n} \to 0$, we have $\tilde{t}^\alpha_{n} \uparrow t$.
    
    For a fixed $T>0$, we consider the subsequence $\{ {\bar{\textnormal{X}}}_{M^\alpha(n_k, T)}(\cdot) \}_{k=0}^\infty$, which satisfies 
    \begin{align*}
        {\bar{\textnormal{X}}}_{M^\alpha(n_k, T)}(0) = {\check{x}}_{M^\alpha(n_k, T)} \ \text{ and }\  {\bar{\textnormal{X}}}_{M^\alpha(n_k, T)}( \widetilde{T}^\alpha_{n_k})= {\check{x}}_{n_k},
    \end{align*}
    where $\widetilde{T}^\alpha_{n} := \Gamma^\alpha_{M^\alpha(n,T), n}$
    
    
    By Lemma~\ref{lem:tight-twotime}, $\{ {\bar{\textnormal{X}}}_{n}(t) \}_{n=1}^\infty$ is tight. Then Prokhorov's theorem (i.e., Proposition~\ref{prop:tight}~\ref{prop:tight:prok}) implies that the subsequence $\{ {\bar{\textnormal{X}}}_{M^\alpha(n_k, T)}(\cdot) \}_{k=0}^\infty$ further has a weakly convergent subsequence.
    Without loss of generality, we assume the subsequence $\{ {\bar{\textnormal{X}}}_{M^\alpha(n_k, T)}(\cdot) \}_{k=0}^\infty$ itself weakly converges.
    Then its initial distribution sequence also converges weakly, i.e., ${\check{x}}_{M^\alpha(n_k, T)} \Rightarrow \mu_T$ for some distribution $\mu_T$.
    Then by Proposition~\ref{prop:mart-prob-approx}, ${\bar{\textnormal{X}}}_{M^\alpha(n_k, T)}(\cdot) \Rightarrow {\textnormal{X}}^{\mu_T}(\cdot) $, where ${\textnormal{X}}^{\mu_T}(\cdot)$ is a solution to \eqref{eq:fclt-twotime:y-sde} with initial distribution $\mu_T$.
    Consequently, we also have ${\bar{\textnormal{X}}}_{M^\alpha(n_k, T)}(T) \Rightarrow {\textnormal{X}}^{\mu_T}(T)$.
    Moreover, recall that we have verified the second condition of Proposition~\ref{prop:tight-suff-slow} in the proof of Lemma~\ref{lem:tight-twotime}. Then $|T - \widetilde{T}^\alpha_{n_k}| \to 0$ implies that $\left\| {\bar{\textnormal{X}}}_{M^\alpha(n_k, T)}(\widetilde{T}^\alpha_{n_k}) - {\bar{\textnormal{X}}}_{M^\alpha(n_k, T)}(T) \right\| \overset{p}{\rightarrow} 0$ as $k \to \infty$. 
    By Slutsky's theorem,
    ${\bar{\textnormal{X}}}_{M^\alpha(n_k, T)}(\widetilde{T}^\alpha_{n_k}) \Rightarrow {\textnormal{X}}^{\mu_T}(T)$, i.e., ${\check{x}}_{n_k} \Rightarrow {\textnormal{X}}^{\mu_T}(T)$. 
    Since ${\check{x}}_{n_k} \Rightarrow \tilde\pi$, this implies that for any $T > 0$, ${\textnormal{X}}^{\mu_T}(T) \sim  \tilde{\pi}$.
    
    \vspace{0.1cm}
    
    \textbf{Part (ii)}.
    Next, we apply ${\check{x}}_{M^\alpha(n_k, T)} \Rightarrow \mu_T$ and ${\textnormal{X}}^{\mu_T}(T) \sim  \tilde{\pi}$ to prove $\tilde\pi = \pi^\star $.
    
    
    Since $\{ {\check{x}}_{n} \}_{n=1}^\infty$ is tight,  for any ${\varepsilon} > 0$, there exists a compact set $K_{\varepsilon} \subset {\mathbb R}^{d_x}$ only depending on ${\varepsilon}$ such that $\sup_{n \ge 0} {\mathbb P}({\check{x}}_{n} \in K_{\varepsilon}) \ge 1 - {\varepsilon}$.
    It follows that $\mu_T(K_{\varepsilon}) \ge 1-{\varepsilon}$ for any $T > 0$.
    Moreover,
    
    Proposition~\ref{prop:ergo} implies that for a fixed $g \in C_c^2({\mathbb R}^{d_x})$, we can find $T_{\varepsilon}$ such that 
    \begin{equation}\label{eq:erg_diff}
        \sup_{{x} \in K_{\varepsilon}} \left| {\mathcal P}_{T_{\varepsilon}}\, g({x})- {\mathbb E}_{{\textnormal{X}} \sim \pi^\star}\, g({\textnormal{X}}) \right| \le {\varepsilon},
    \end{equation}
    where ${\mathcal P}_t$ represents a semigroup induced by the SDE in \eqref{eq:fclt-twotime:y-sde}, that is, 
    \begin{align}\label{eq:semigroup}
        {\mathcal P}_t f(x) = {\mathbb E} [ f({\textnormal{X}}(t)) \,|\, {\textnormal{X}}(0) = x ],
    \end{align}
    where ${\textnormal{X}}(\cdot)$ is the solution to the SDE in \eqref{eq:fclt-twotime:y-sde}. 
    Setting $T = T_{\varepsilon}$, we have ${\textnormal{X}}^{\mu_{T_{\varepsilon}}}(T_{\varepsilon}) \sim  \tilde{\pi}$.
    
    
    Since ${\textnormal{X}}^{\mu_{T_{\varepsilon}}}(\cdot)$ is a solution to \eqref{eq:fclt-twotime:x-sde} with initial distribution $\mu_{T_{\varepsilon}}$,  we have
    \begin{align*}
        {\mathbb E}_{{\textnormal{X}} \sim \tilde\pi}\, g({\textnormal{X}})
        = {\mathbb E}\, [ g ({\textnormal{X}}^{\mu_{T_{\varepsilon}}}(T_{\varepsilon}) ) \,|\, {\textnormal{X}}(0) \sim \mu_{T_{\varepsilon}} ]
        \overset{\eqref{eq:semigroup}}{=} \int_{{\mathbb R}^{d_x}} {\mathcal P}_{T_{\varepsilon}}\, g({x}) d \mu_{T_{\varepsilon}}({x})
    \end{align*}
    It follows that
    \begin{equation*}
        
        \begin{aligned}
            \left| {\mathbb E}_{{\textnormal{X}} \sim \tilde\pi}\, g({\textnormal{X}}) - {\mathbb E}_{{\textnormal{X}} \sim \pi^\star}\, g({\textnormal{X}}) \right|
            
            & \le \int_{{\mathbb R}^{d_x}} \left| {\mathcal P}_{T_{\varepsilon}} g({x}) -{\mathbb E}_{{\textnormal{X}} \sim \pi^\star} g({\textnormal{X}}) \right| d \mu_{T_{\varepsilon}}({x})\\ 
            & = \int_{K_{\varepsilon}} \left| {\mathcal P}_{T_{\varepsilon}} g({x}) - {\mathbb E}_{{\textnormal{X}} \sim \pi^\star} g({\textnormal{X}}) \right| d \mu_{T_{\varepsilon}}({x}) \\
            & \qquad + \int_{K_{\varepsilon}^c} \left| {\mathcal P}_{T_{\varepsilon}} g({x}) - {\mathbb E}_{{\textnormal{X}} \sim \pi^\star} g({\textnormal{X}}) \right| d \mu_{T_{\varepsilon}}({x}) \\
            &\le \int_{K_{\varepsilon}} \left| {\mathcal P}_{T_{\varepsilon}} g({x}) - {\mathbb E}_{{\textnormal{X}} \sim \pi^\star} g({\textnormal{X}}) \right| d \mu_{T_{\varepsilon}}({x}) + 2 \|g\|_\infty \mu_{T_{\varepsilon}} (K_{\varepsilon}^c) \\ 
            & \overset{(a)}{\le} {\varepsilon} + 2\|g\|_\infty {\varepsilon},
        \end{aligned}
    \end{equation*}
    where (a) is due to $\mu_{T_{\varepsilon}}(K_{\varepsilon}) \ge 1-{\varepsilon}$ and \eqref{eq:erg_diff}.
    Letting ${\varepsilon} \to \infty$, we obtain ${\mathbb E}_{{\textnormal{X}} \sim \tilde\pi}\, g({\textnormal{X}}) = {\mathbb E}_{{\textnormal{X}} \sim \pi^\star}\, g({\textnormal{X}}) $.
    For any $g \in C_c^2({\mathbb R}^{d_x})$, we can repeat the above procedure, implying $\tilde\pi = \pi^\star$.
    \vspace{0.2cm}
    
    \textbf{Step~3: concluding whole sequence convergence}. This step is straightforward.
    In Steps~1 and 2, we have verified the all the conditions in Proposition~\ref{prop:mart-prob-approx}.
    Moreover, ${\bar{\textnormal{X}}}_{n}(0)  \Rightarrow \pi^\star$, the invariant distribution of \eqref{eq:fclt-twotime:x-sde}.
    Consequently, ${\bar{\textnormal{X}}}_{n}(\cdot)$ converges weakly to the solution of \eqref{eq:fclt-twotime:x-sde} with the initial distribution $\pi^\star$, implying that this solution is a stationary process.
    Since $B_1$ is a Hurwitz matrix, the invariant distribution $\pi^\star={\mathcal N}(0, \Sigma_{x})$ with $\Sigma_x$ satisfying the equation in \eqref{eq:fclt-twotime:x-var} \cite[Section~6.5]{risken1996fokker}.

Under the tightness in Lemma~\ref{lem:tight-twotime}, 
    Proposition~\ref{prop:tight} shows that it suffices to examine the finite-dimensional distributions of ${\bar{\textnormal{Y}}}_{n}(\cdot)$.
    
    Recall that ${\check{z}}_{n}$ is defined as ${\check{z}}_{n} = {\check{y}}_{n} - \sqrt{ \kappa_{n-1} } B_2 B_1^{-1} {\check{x}}_{n}$ with $\kappa_{n-1} = \beta_{n-1} / \alpha_{n-1} = o(1)$; Assumption~\ref{assump:mart-decouple-rate} implies ${\mathbb E} \| {\check{x}}_{n} \|^2 = {\mathcal O}(1)$.
    
    It follows that ${\check{y}}_{n} - {\check{z}}_{n} \overset{p}{\to} 0$.
    
    
    
    Meanwhile, from the definition in \eqref{eq:def:ybar} and \eqref{eq:def:zbar}, for each fixed $t$, ${\bar{\textnormal{Y}}}_{n}(t) - {\bar{\textnormal{Z}}}_{n}(t)$ is the linear combination of ${\check{y}}_{N^\beta(n,t)} -  {\check{z}}_{N^\beta(n,t)}$ and ${\check{y}}_{N^\beta(n,t)+1} -  {\check{z}}_{N^\beta(n,t)+1}$, both converging to the zero vector in probability.
    Consequently, ${\bar{\textnormal{Y}}}_{n}(t) - {\bar{\textnormal{Z}}}_{n}(t) \overset{p}{\to} 0$. 
    Similarly, we could prove that for any positive integer $k$ and $t_1, \ldots, t_k$,
    $({\bar{\textnormal{Y}}}_{n}(t_1) - {\bar{\textnormal{Z}}}_{n}(t_1), \dots, {\bar{\textnormal{Y}}}_{n}(t_k) - {\bar{\textnormal{Z}}}_{n} (t_k) ) \overset{p}{\to} 0$.
    Applying Slutsky's theorem and Theorem~\ref{thm:fclt-twotime}, we obtain that the finite-dimensional distributions of ${\bar{\textnormal{Y}}}_{n}(\cdot)$ converge weakly to the finite-dimensional distributions of the stationary distribution of \eqref{eq:fclt-twotime:y-sde}.
    Consequently, ${\bar{\textnormal{Y}}}_{n}(\cdot)$ converges weakly to the stationary distribution of \eqref{eq:fclt-twotime:y-sde}.
    
    Note that Assumption~\ref{assump:hurwitz} implies that $-\left(B_3 - \frac{\tilde{\beta}}{2} {I} \right)$ is a Hurwitz matrix.
    The property of the SDE in \eqref{eq:fclt-twotime:y-sde} implies that the invariant distribution is ${\mathcal N}(0, \Sigma_{y})$ with $\Sigma_y$ satisfying the equation in \eqref{eq:fclt-twotime:y-var} in \cite[Section~6.5]{risken1996fokker}.

nodes.name: Proof of Corollary~\ref{cor:clt}
nodes.statement: From the definition of checkx_n, we have alpha_n-1^-1/2 hatx_n Rightarrow mathcal N(0, Sigma_x). Assumption~ ensures that alpha_n-1 / alpha_n to 1. Then Slutsky's theorem implies alpha_n^-1/2 hatx_n Rightarrow mathcal N(0, Sigma_x). Similarly, we could prove beta_n^-1/2 haty_n Rightarrow mathcal N(0, Sigma_y). Moreover, since x^star = H(y^star), we have alpha_n^-1/2 (x_n - x^star) = alpha_n^-1/2 hatx_n + alpha_n^-1/2 (H(y_n) - H(y^star)). Using the delta method, we have beta_n^-1/2 (H(y_n) - H(y^star)) Rightarrow mathcal N(0, H^star Sigma_y (H^star)^top ) with H^star = nabla H(y^star) in mathbb R^d_x times d_y. Since beta_n / alpha_n to 0, applying Slutsky's theorem yields alpha_n^-1/2 (H(y_n) - H(y^star)) Rightarrow 0 . Consequently, alpha_n^-1/2 (x_n - x^star) Rightarrow mathcal N(0, Sigma_x).

    Assumption~\ref{assump:stepsize-twotime} ensures that $\alpha_{n-1} / \alpha_{n} \to 1$.
    Then Slutsky's theorem implies $\alpha_{n}^{-1/2} {\hat{x}}_{n} \Rightarrow {\mathcal N}(0, \Sigma_x)$.
    Similarly, we could prove $\beta_{n}^{-1/2} {\hat{y}}_{n} \Rightarrow {\mathcal N}(0, \Sigma_y)$.
